title: The even-exponent Erdős–Moser equation
summary: Can a positive even power ever equal the sum of all smaller nonnegative integers raised to the same power? Ruling this out would settle the remaining case of the Erdős–Moser conjecture.

tasks.title: Restrict the base of a hypothetical solution
tasks.claim:
∀ k m : ℕ, 2 ≤ k → Even k → 2 ≤ m → powerSum k m = m ^ k →
    3 < m ∧ m % 8 = 3
tasks.role: Isolates the residue class in which an even-exponent solution could occur.
tasks.context: Use Moree's proof of Moser's theorem (https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.2940). Compare the sum and m^k modulo 4 to restrict m modulo 8. For an even m, grouping the sum into blocks modulo its exact power of two gives a nonzero residue, contradicting m^k. Handle m=3 separately using 1+2^k < 3^k for k≥2.

tasks.title: Restrict the exponent using the prime divisors
tasks.claim: ∀ k m : ℕ, 2 ≤ k → Even k → 2 ≤ m → powerSum k m = m ^ k → MoserPrimeDivisors k m
tasks.role: Adds a constraint on the exponent for every prime dividing one of four integers near the base.
tasks.context: Use the finite-field power sum in Moree, Sections 2 and 4 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.2940). For m−1 and m+1, reduce complete blocks modulo p. For 2m−1 and 2m+1, pair opposite residues using even k. In each case the equation forces a nonzero residue, so the power-sum identity gives p−1 ∣ k. For p=2 the divisibility holds directly.

tasks.title: Exclude solutions in the remaining residue class
tasks.claim: ∀ k m : ℕ, 2 ≤ k → Even k → 3 < m → m % 8 = 3 → MoserPrimeDivisors k m → powerSum k m ≠ m ^ k
tasks.role: Would rule out every candidate left by Moser's restriction.
tasks.context: This is the open step. With the prime divisor restriction supplied as a hypothesis, try to combine the four reciprocal-sum congruences in Moree, Sections 2 and 4 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.2940). The published combination gives finite lower bounds. A contradiction has to cover arbitrarily large m. Record any narrower provable claim in a give-up report.
